title: Oil Prices Drop After U.S. and Iran Pause Fighting for a Second Day
summary: No strikes have been reported from either side since Friday, leaving oil investors optimistic about a resolution to the conflict.
body_text: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT You have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load. Oil prices fell and stocks wavered on Monday as fighting between the United States and Iran paused. The relative calm left investors hopeful that more energy might soon start flowing from the region, even though ships still faced dangerous conditions. Energy prices had surged throughout most of July as the cease-fire between the countries fell apart. Then, last week, oil topped $100 a barrel after the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, broadened the conflict by threatening a blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. But President Trump’s decision to hold off , at least temporarily, on a major escalation of the war brought renewed optimism among traders about a resolution. Here is the latest: Oil prices drop. Shipping traffic reflects continued caution. Global stocks rise modestly. Gasoline prices hover above $4 a gallon. What they are saying: Despite the lull, ’the situation remains highly fluid.’ Oil prices drop. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, fell 8.7 percent, to $88.36 a barrel. That is for oil to be delivered in September. West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, fell 7.5 percent to $82.61 a barrel for September delivery. Investors and analysts are focused on the continued disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz , the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman, as well as threats to another strait, the Bab al-Mandab , at the mouth of the Red Sea. title: The Best Rollout Platforms Put Control Back in Your Hands
summary: There’s an assumption built into a lot of enterprise software that gets accepted without much pushback: if the platform is powerful, you’ll need outside help to run it. A partner to configure it. A partner to change it. A partner to keep it running the way you need it to. That assumption isn’t a law […]
body_text: There’s an assumption built into a lot of enterprise software that gets accepted without much pushback: if the platform is powerful, you’ll need outside help to run it. A partner to configure it. A partner to change it. A partner to keep it running the way you need it to. That assumption isn’t a law of physics. It’s a design choice, and it’s worth questioning if your team is currently living inside it. Where the assumption comes from Plenty of deployment and asset management platforms are built on large, general-purpose CRM ecosystems. That foundation makes them flexible in theory, but flexible in a way that requires specialized expertise to unlock. Configuration isn’t a settings menu your ops team can open. It’s a project, usually scoped and delivered by a certified implementation partner, because the underlying system wasn’t built for a non-technical user to configure directly. Once that pattern is in place, it doesn’t go away after go-live. Every new asset type, every workflow tweak, every reporting change routes back through the same partner relationship. Your team ends up fluent in describing what they need, but never actually building it themselves. What “self-managed” actually means The alternative isn’t a less capable platform. It’s one built from the start to be configured by the people running the work, not a certified specialist. That means your ops lead can add a new site template without a scoping call. Your PM can adjust a workflow stage without a change request. Your reporting can reflect exactly how your team tracks a project, not a generic template a consultant thought was close enough. This isn’t a hypothetical trade-off between power and simplicity. It’s a question of who holds the keys. A self-managed platform means your team holds them, and that changes both the speed of onboarding and the cost of every adjustment afterward. Why this matters more as you scale A five-person team can tolerate an inflexible system because there’s not much complexity to manage yet. A team running hundreds of sites, with field crews, project managers, and leadership all needing different views of the same data, can’t. That’s exactly the point where an inflexible, partner-dependent platform stops being a minor annoyance and starts being a real drag on delivery timelines. If your team is already asking a partner to make changes a competent internal admin should be able to make directly, that’s usually the clearest sign the platform wasn’t built with your team in mind. The real question to ask Before your next platform decision, or before renewing your current one, ask a simple question: if we needed to change something tomorrow, could our own team do it, or would we need to call someone first? If the answer is “call someone,” that’s not flexibility. That’s dependency dressed up as configurability. A rollout platform should put control back in the hands of the people closest to the work, not route every decision through a third party who wasn’t in the room when the problem came up. title: Closing the Compliance Gap: How Fragmented Provider Data Creates Hidden Regulatory Exposure
summary: Fragmented provider data creates hidden regulatory exposure. Learn how governance, automation, and a single source of truth reduce healthcare compliance risk.
body_text: SUMMARY ​Fragmented provider data makes it harder to keep information accurate, consistent, and compliant across an organization. ​Disconnected systems, duplicate records, and manual processes increase audit, regulatory, and operational risk. ​A single source of truth, backed by governance and automation, helps organizations improve data accuracy and stay audit-ready. ​Why accurate provider data is essential for compliance and audit readiness ​Provider data management sits at the center of nearly every operational and regulatory function in a health plan. Credentialing, contracting, enrollment, directory management, and compliance reporting all depend on accurate, consistent provider records. Yet many organizations maintain this information across disconnected systems, each operating with its own data standards and update cycles. ​This fragmentation often looks like a data management problem, but left unaddressed, it becomes a healthcare compliance risk. Governance, automation, and a single source of truth are foundational to closing that gap. ​The growing regulatory focus on data accuracy ​Regulators are focusing increased scrutiny on provider directory accuracy, particularly as inaccurate directories directly affect member access to care. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and state regulators have tied compliance requirements to the accuracy and timeliness of provider directory regulations, with penalties for plans that fail to meet update frequency standards. ​The consequences extend beyond directory errors. When provider records are inaccurate, members may be directed to providers who are unavailable, out-of-network, or no longer accepting patients. This creates access-to-care failures with real regulatory and reputational consequences. ​Compliance risks extend beyond credentialing ​Provider credentialing is often where data accuracy issues first come to light, but the impact extends across the entire provider data lifecycle. Contracting terms rely on verified credentials. Reimbursement accuracy depends on current participation status. Healthcare audit readiness requires consistent, traceable records across systems. A credentialing error that goes uncorrected doesn't just stay in the credentialing system — it propagates. ​Where fragmented provider data creates hidden risk ​Credentialing systems operating in isolation ​When credentialing compliance systems don't connect to other operational systems, expired licenses and inconsistent credential records can persist undetected. Duplicate provider profiles are common, and they create conflicting records that make it difficult to know which version of a provider's information is accurate. ​Disconnected provider directories ​Outdated provider information in public directories is one of the most visible compliance failures. Provider directory accuracy requirements are strict, and regulators expect timely updates. When directory systems don't receive automatic updates from credentialing or enrollment systems, errors can accumulate, and regulatory penalties follow. ​Contracting and enrollment data misalignment ​Conflicting provider records between contracting and provider enrollment data systems create incorrect participation status, delayed onboarding, and network update failures. These misalignments slow operations and introduce billing and reimbursement risks. ​Manual data handoffs and spreadsheets ​Manual processes introduce human error at every level. Without automated workflows, there's limited visibility into data changes and no reliable audit trail. This makes it nearly impossible to demonstrate data accuracy during a healthcare audit. ​The real cost of provider data fragmentation ​Regulatory exposure ​Provider data compliance failures result in compliance violations, fines, and corrective action plans. Repeated findings can trigger increased regulatory oversight, compounding the administrative burden for staff and reputational damage to the organization. ​Operational inefficiency ​Fragmented data forces duplicate work across teams. Provider onboarding slows when enrollment and credentialing systems don't share information. In turn, administrative costs rise as staff manually reconcile conflicting records. ​Audit challenges ​Without centralized, traceable records, proving provider data integrity during an audit is difficult. Missing documentation and limited historical records are among the most common findings in payer compliance reviews. ​Reputational risk ​Provider dissatisfaction grows when onboarding is delayed or participation status is incorrectly recorded. Members lose trust when directory information is inaccurate. Both of these outcomes carry long-term consequences for network stability and public perception. ​Building a single source of truth for provider data ​What a single source of truth actually means ​Establishing a single source of truth for provider data means creating a centralized provider record that all departments can access, update, and rely on. It requires consistent data standards and shared visibility across credentialing, contracting, enrollment, and compliance teams. ​Connecting the provider data lifecycle ​Healthcare provider data lifecycle management spans recruitment, credentialing, enrollment, contracting, directory management, ongoing monitoring, and compliance reporting. A connected approach ensures that updates made at any stage are reflected across all systems in real time, reducing the risk of outdated or conflicting records. ​Eliminating duplicate and conflicting records ​Improving provider data accuracy across systems requires data standardization, clear governance policies, and defined data stewardship practices. Organizations need to know who owns each data element, what the authoritative source is, and how conflicts are resolved. ​Aligning governance, automation, and compliance ​Establishing provider data governance frameworks ​A provider data governance framework for health plans defines ownership, accountability, data quality standards, and escalation processes. Without clear governance, data accuracy depends on individual effort rather than systematic controls. ​Leveraging automation to reduce risk ​Provider data automation reduces reliance on manual processes through automated validation workflows, credential monitoring, directory synchronization, and exception management. Automation doesn't eliminate the need for human oversight, but it makes that oversight far more efficient and reliable. ​Creating ongoing data quality controls ​Routine audits, accuracy scoring, compliance dashboards, and continuous monitoring form the foundation of sustainable data quality management. These controls allow organizations to identify and address issues before they become regulatory findings. ​Preparing for audits before they happen ​What regulators and auditors expect ​Auditors and regulatory bodies expect documentation, consistency, traceability, and timely updates. Organizations that can demonstrate a clear provider data lifecycle with documented changes and standardized workflows are far better positioned than those relying on manual records. ​Creating an audit-ready provider data environment ​Healthcare audit readiness best practices include centralized reporting, automated change tracking, standardized documentation workflows, and real-time access to compliance data. These capabilities reduce the time and effort required to respond to audit requests. ​Measuring compliance readiness ​Key performance indicators for compliance management include directory accuracy rates, credentialing turnaround time, data quality scores, exception resolution rates, and audit findings reduction. Tracking these metrics consistently gives leaders early warning of emerging risk. ​ Strategic questions compliance and data leaders should be asking ​Can we trust our provider data across systems? ​If different systems contain different versions of the same provider record, the answer is no. Risks of fragmented provider data grow every time a discrepancy goes unresolved. ​Do we have clear ownership and governance? ​Improving provider data governance starts with defining who is accountable for data accuracy at each stage of the provider lifecycle and what standards apply across systems. ​Are we able to demonstrate compliance at any time? ​Provider directory compliance requirements and credentialing standards don't pause for audit preparation cycles. Organizations need to maintain a continuous state of readiness, not a reactive one. ​Where are manual processes introducing risk? ​Every manual handoff is a potential point of failure. Mapping those handoffs is the first step toward replacing them with automated, auditable workflows. ​Closing the compliance gap with connected provider data ​Fragmented provider data management creates risks that often remain invisible until audits, complaints, or regulatory reviews surface them. Organizations that establish a single source of truth, supported by governance and automation, are better positioned to maintain compliance, reduce operational costs, and strengthen audit readiness. ​Regulatory expectations around provider data governance and healthcare regulatory compliance continue to grow more specific. Accurate provider data is no longer simply an operational concern — it's a strategic compliance requirement. ​FAQs ​What is provider data fragmentation? ​Provider data fragmentation occurs when provider information is stored across multiple disconnected systems, such as credentialing, contracting, enrollment, and directory systems, without consistent standards or real-time synchronization. ​Why does fragmented provider data create compliance risk? ​Disconnected systems produce conflicting or outdated records that affect credentialing, directories, contracting, and audits. These inaccuracies can result in regulatory violations, fines, and corrective action requirements. ​What is a single source of truth for provider data? ​​A single source of truth is a centralized provider record with consistent data standards and shared visibility across all departments, ensuring that every system reflects the same accurate information. How can healthcare organizations improve provider data governance? ​Organizations can improve provider data governance by defining clear data ownership, establishing quality standards, implementing escalation processes, and using automated validation to maintain accuracy across the provider data lifecycle. ​ What role does automation play in provider data compliance? ​Provider data automation helps organizations keep provider records accurate, current, and aligned across systems through validation, monitoring, and synchronization. It also creates auditable records that support compliance reporting and regulatory reviews. ​How does provider data quality impact audit readiness? ​Poor provider data integrity makes it difficult to produce consistent, traceable documentation during audits. High-quality, centrally managed data enables organizations to demonstrate compliance accurately and efficiently. ‍

title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 travel guide and attendee tips
summary: Plan for TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 with hotel recommendations, budgeting tips, agenda planning, networking advice, and SoMa dining near Moscone West.
body_text: Key takeaways TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is Oct. 13–15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. This guide walks through SoMa hotels, SFO transfers, GSA budgeting, Expo strategy, and departure logistics for the three-day program. Hotels within walking distance of Moscone West fill up quickly for Disrupt week, so compare SoMa, the Financial District, and Union Square before booking. Conference-week hotel rates often exceed San Francisco's federal lodging per diem, so budget for the difference or stay a little farther from the venue. Navan Edge — the personal assistant forbusiness travel — books your flights, hotels, and restaurant reservations in a single chat based on live availability and your personal preferences. Prioritize the sessions that matter most, but leave time for Startup Battlefield, the Deal Flow Café, the Disrupt Expo Hall, and the conversations where partnerships and funding opportunities often begin. Send follow-up notes within a few days of the conference ending while pitch feedback and investor intros are still fresh. TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 brings founders, investors, operators, and startup teams to Moscone West for three days of product launches, fundraising conversations, and practical sessions on building and scaling companies.[1][2] Your conference pass gets you into keynotes, Startup Battlefield, and the Disrupt Expo Hall. The decisions you make before and between sessions shape the value you take home. A well-planned week can leave you with stronger investor relationships, clearer product direction, and actionable next steps instead of conference fatigue and missed opportunities. What is TechCrunch Disrupt and who is it for? TechCrunch Disrupt is TechCrunch's flagship startup and technology conference, bringing founders, investors, and operators together for three days of pitching, deal-making, and product insights.[1] The 2026 event runs Oct. 13–15 at Moscone West in San Francisco.[1][2] TechCrunch expects more than 10,000 attendees, with the audience spanning early-stage founders pitching in Startup Battlefield, growth-stage CEOs scaling their companies, investors sourcing new opportunities, and operators looking for practical sessions on hiring, AI infrastructure, and go-to-market strategy.[1] Disrupt also welcomes corporate innovators, sponsors, and accredited media.[1][3] The agenda includes more than 200 sessions across six stages, with more than 250 speakers covering startups, AI, venture capital, and emerging technology.[4] If you're building the business case for attending, focus on measurable outcomes: scheduling investor meetings before you arrive, evaluating potential partners on the Expo floor, or refining your fundraising narrative before your next funding round. What makes TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 worth the trip TechCrunch Disrupt is where founders, investors, and operators come together to share ideas, evaluate new technologies, and build the relationships that shape the next stage of a company. For founders, that means Startup Battlefield, investor Q&A, and opportunities to refine a fundraising story. Investors come to discover emerging companies and build new relationships, while operators come for practical sessions on hiring, AI, go-to-market strategy, and scaling a growing business. Some of the highest-value experiences happen away from the main stages: Disrupt Expo Hall: Explore sponsor booths, product demonstrations, and startup showcases across the show floor.[3] Startup Battlefield: Watch startups compete live for equity-free prize money and industry recognition.[1][5] Deal Flow Café: Meet founders and investors through curated networking available to qualifying pass holders.[3] Braindates: Join one-on-one and small-group peer conversations scheduled through the event app.[3] Side events: Attend partner-hosted networking events, receptions, and meetups throughout Disrupt week.[1] Six conference stages: Choose from sessions across the Builders, Industry, Breakout, Roundtable, and other programming tracks.[4] The value of TechCrunch Disrupt comes from what happens after the conference. Stronger investor relationships, clearer product direction, and new partnerships can all help move your business forward once you're back at work. Planning your travel, agenda, and meetings before you arrive makes it much easier to spend your time on those outcomes instead of conference logistics. Where to stay for TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Your hotel location shapes how easy it is to get to Moscone West, meet up with colleagues between sessions, and attend evening networking events throughout conference week. Staying within walking distance makes it easier to get between sessions, networking events, and your hotel throughout the conference. Hotels by distance to Moscone West Choosing the right neighborhood is about more than hotel quality. A property a few extra blocks from Moscone West may cost less while still keeping you within easy walking distance of sessions and networking events. Area Distance to venue Details Rates SoMa/Moscone adjacency 3–8 minutes walking Closest blocks with shortest path to keynotes and Disrupt Expo Hall Highest during conference week Financial District/Embarcadero 10–15 minutes walking Quieter rooms, stronger dinner options; favored by investors and exec dinners Higher, with better availability Union Square/Mid-Market 12–20 minutes walking or short Muni ride More availability, with a slightly longer commute Moderate to high; fills up later than SoMa When comparing hotels, look beyond the nightly rate. Parking, destination fees, taxes, and cancellation policies can change the total cost of your stay. Booking in SoMa shortens your commute to keynotes and Expo appointments. Financial District and Embarcadero properties trade a short walk for quieter nights and polished client-dinner options. Union Square works when Moscone-adjacent blocks sell out, but confirm Muni or BART access before booking farther away. TechCrunch Disrupt hotel pricing Navan analyzed anonymized hotel booking patterns near Moscone West during TechCrunch Disrupt week in October 2025.[13] Use these benchmarks to put pricing into context: Median hotel rate: During conference week, the median nightly rate near the venue was $493 — about 27% higher than a typical October week in the same area (median of $387). Stay length: Business travelers stayed an average of 3.9 nights. Check-in pattern: Sunday was the most common arrival day, and Friday the most common departure day. Late bookings: Roughly 35% of bookings were made within two weeks of check-in. What stands out: According to Navan data, travelers who booked 1–2 months before check-in paid a median of $409 per night, while waiting until the final 1–2 weeks pushed the median to $535.[13] That's a difference of about $126 per night, making earlier booking the safer strategy if your travel policy allows. TechCrunch Disrupt flight trends The primary airport serving TechCrunch Disrupt attendees is San Francisco International Airport (SFO). Navan flight data from Disrupt week 2025 shows 3,406 business flights into San Francisco, with 17.6% arriving from international origins.[13] The busiest origin cities were New York, Newark, Chicago, Seattle, and Denver. Consider arriving on Oct. 12, if your travel policy allows. You'll have time to settle into your hotel and ease into the week before the conference begins. Book your TechCrunch Disrupt travel through Navan Edge Navan Edge coordinates flights, hotels, and restaurant reservations in one conversation, using your preferences and live inventory. For TechCrunch Disrupt, ask Navan Edge to compare Moscone-adjacent rooms against Financial District and Union Square alternatives with the amenities you need , then book your SFO flight in the same thread. You can stack three reward layers in a single bookingthrough Navan Edge, including hotel loyalty points (earned as if you booked direct), credit card multipliers, and 5% back in Amazon Gift Cards on eligible hotel stays. The Loyalty Wallet keeps your program statuses and progress (including air miles) in one place. For a deeper look at the mechanics, see our guide on how to earn travel rewards on business trips . Set your San Francisco budget before traveling The cost of attending TechCrunch Disrupt goes well beyond airfare and accommodations. Factor your conference pass, hotel, meals outside conference programming, airport transportation, client dinners, and other business travel expenses into your budget before you book. Federal per diem for San Francisco The U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) sets federal per diem rates by city and season. At the time of publication, the following October rates for FY2026 to San Francisco (city and county):[6] $364 per day: Includes $272 per night for lodging and $92 per day for meals and incidental expenses (M&IE) M&IE breakdown: $23 for breakfast, $26 for lunch, $38 for dinner, and $5 for incidentals (deduct conference-provided meals from your meal claim as applicable) First and last travel days: Includes M&IE allowance of $69 (i.e. 75% of the daily M&IE rate) Updated rates for FY2027 (October 2026–September 2027) are expected to be published in mid-August 2026 at gsa.gov. During conference week, hotels within walking distance of Moscone West often exceed the federal lodging rate ($272 per night), so budget for the difference or confirm with finance before booking. Additional expenses Before you travel, estimate your daily spending so there are fewer surprises when it's time to submit your expense report. Conference registration: Early Bird Attendee Passes start at $559, Founder Passes at $579, and Investor Passes at $799, with additional discounted tiers available for students, nonprofits, and Expo+ attendees. Verify current pricing before registering.[3] Airport transportation: BART from SFO to Powell Street or Montgomery Street costs about $11, while rideshares typically run $35–$50 depending on traffic and surge pricing.[7][8] Client dinners: SoMa steakhouses and private dining rooms typically run $75–$175 per person. After-hours networking: Partner receptions, investor events, team outings, and other unofficial gatherings can add to your travel budget beyond conference-provided meals. Map these line items before purchase, so approvals and your post-trip expense report stay clean. Plan your TechCrunch Disrupt agenda TechCrunch has published the Disrupt 2026 agenda, giving attendees time to explore sessions across six stages before the conference begins.[4][14] The program includes more than 200 sessions covering startups, AI, venture capital, product development, and scaling businesses.[1][4] Tuesday (Oct. 13): Startup Battlefield rounds, Industry Stage sessions on payments and fintech, and Builders Stage panels including “What Happens When OpenAI Ships Your Roadmap” and “Winning Pre-Seed Without a Product”[14] Wednesday (Oct. 14): Additional Startup Battlefield sessions, AI-focused Industry Stage programming, and Builders Stage discussions, including “M&A Is Now an Early-Stage Strategy”[14] Thursday (Oct. 15): Closing Startup Battlefield rounds and Builders Stage sessions including “The 90-Day GTM: Why $0–$10M ARR Is the New Baseline” and “How to Create Viral Growth and Capitalize On It”[14][15] Featured programming spans pre-seed fundraising, product-market fit, AI, hiring, compensation, and go-to-market strategy, with additional speakers and sessions announced closer to the event.[15] Build flexibility into your schedule Start by reviewing the published agenda and identifying your highest-priority sessions.[14] Leave room between sessions for Startup Battlefield, the Disrupt Expo Hall, Braindates, Deal Flow Café meetings, and the conversations that often become the most valuable part of the conference. Here are some tips to prepare for Disrupt: Sessions: Star your must-attend sessions in the event app and check for updates as additional programming is announced. Meetings: Reach out to investors, partners, or fellow founders about two weeks before the conference to schedule short meetings while everyone is in San Francisco. Logistics: Download the Disrupt app, enable session alerts, and set your out-of-office message. Networking: Decide how you'll exchange contact information and add a quick note after each conversation to make follow-up easier. For more tips on getting ready for your trip, read our business trip planning guide covering flights, hotels, and departure checklists. What to pack and wear at TechCrunch Disrupt Business casual is the norm at TechCrunch Disrupt. Think clean blazers over tees or button-downs, dark jeans or chinos, comfortable closed-toe shoes, and a light layer to manage chilly session rooms. If you're pitching, meeting investors, or attending client dinners, consider dressing one step sharper than you would for a typical workday.[3] San Francisco in October runs mild in the afternoon, with highs around 68–72°F (20–22°C) and evening fog that can drop temperatures into the mid-50s°F (13–15°C).[2] You'll move between climate-controlled halls and outdoor SoMa walks, so pack breathable daytime fabrics and a sweater or blazer for evening events. Conference essentials While most business travelers remember their tech, they often forget these must-pack items: Two pairs of comfortable shoes: Convention flooring and SoMa distances can be tough on your feet, and switching up shoes can help. Portable charger: Session alerts, Braindate notes, and badge scans can drain batteries by mid-afternoon. Reusable water bottle: Dry convention air dehydrates faster than you notice between sessions. Throat lozenges and hand sanitizer: Crowded keynotes and Expo aisles could mean a lot of exposure to germs over three days. Light layer: Breakout rooms might run cold even when SoMa is mild, so bring layers so you're ready for anything. Earplugs: These are useful for evening events with music and if you're sleeping near noisy areas. Getting from the airport to the TechCrunch Disrupt venue Most attendees arrive via San Francisco International Airport (SFO), roughly 13 miles south of Moscone West.[8] Oakland International (OAK) is a solid Southwest alternative. If your schedule allows, fly in a day early and you'll have plenty of time to settle into your hotel before opening programming. Option Time Cost Notes BART (Yellow/Red line) 30–40 minutes About $11[7] To Powell St or Montgomery St, then roughly 10 minutes walking to Moscone West; runs from 5 a.m.–midnight[7][8] Rideshare (Uber/Lyft) 30–50 minutes About $35–$50[8] Door to door with surge pricing possible during peak arrivals; pickup on Level 5 domestic garage[8] Taxi 30–50 minutes About $45–$60 Curbside pickup; flat-meter pricing, but travel time fluctuates with traffic OAK + BART 45–60 minutes About $12–$15 Lower cost but has the longest travel time For solo weekday arrivals with a rolling bag, BART is usually the fastest and cheapest door-to-near-door option. Rideshare works when you're landing late, traveling with a group, or staying outside downtown. Beyond sessions: Make time for the Disrupt Expo Hall and hallway conversations Some of the most valuable conversations at TechCrunch Disrupt happen outside the session rooms. Plan plenty of time to explore the Disrupt Expo Hall, attend Startup Battlefield, and connect with founders, investors, and partners between sessions. Disrupt Expo Hall: Explore sponsor booths, product demonstrations, startup showcases, and technology activations throughout the show floor.[3] Startup Battlefield: Watch startups pitch live, hear feedback from judges, and see emerging companies compete throughout the conference.[1][5] Deal Flow Café: Meet founders and investors through curated networking available to qualifying pass holders.[3] Braindates: Join one-on-one and small-group conversations with other attendees through the event app.[3] Side events: Attend partner-hosted receptions, dinners, demos, and networking events throughout Disrupt week.[1] Make networking part of your plan As enticing as back-to-back sessions can be, a few thoughtful conversations can be more valuable than an overflowing schedule. Before you travel: Make a short list of investors, founders, partners, or customers you'd like to meet, then reach out before the conference to schedule time together. During the conference: After each conversation, jot down a quick note about what you discussed and any agreed-upon next steps. You'll thank yourself when it's time to follow up. At the end of each day: Spend a few minutes drafting follow-up emails while conversations are still fresh, then send them within a day or two of returning home. Finally, leave yourself some breathing room. A quieter moment between sessions or a short walk away from Moscone West can leave you with more energy for the conversations and ideas you'll remember long after the conference ends. What to eat at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Conference days at TechCrunch Disrupt can stretch from early sessions through evening networking events, so plan your meals before you arrive. We recommend starting each day with a filling breakfast, carrying water and a high-protein snack in your bag, and not relying on grabbing food between sessions when the Disrupt Expo Hall is busy. If you're hosting clients or meeting investors over dinner, reserve restaurants using Navan Edge in the same chat thread where you booked your hotel and flights. For sit-down meals beyond quick coffee breaks and convention snacks, these SoMa restaurants work well for different Disrupt moments: Client dinner: Fogo de Chão on 3rd Street can be good for executive dinners with private rooms and AV for larger groups steps from Moscone.[9] Investor one-on-one: MKT Restaurant & Bar at the Four Seasons on Market Street suits polished business lunches and dinners near the venue.[10] Team meal: Kaiyo on 3rd Street offers Nikkei cuisine with semi-private dining for mid-size founder teams.[11] Upscale close: Alexander's Steakhouse serves wagyu-focused steaks for high-stakes conversations within a short rideshare of SoMa.[12] Finish strong on departure day Your Disrupt outcomes don't fully count until you're through SFO and back in your normal workflow. Tackle these before checkout Wednesday or Thursday: Pack Wednesday night: Charge gear, stage travel clothes, sweep the room for badges and chargers. Confirm late checkout: If you have an evening flight, organize during check-in at the front desk, and double check a day before. Leave extra time at SFO: Post-conference SFO can get busy — allow at least two hours for domestic flights and three for international. Submit expenses while details are live: Upload receipts before SoMa blurs together, and flag lodging above your per-diem cap when you file. title: Bolt Lock Wins NEMPA Yankee Supplier Award
summary: The New England Motor Press Association (NEMPA) selected BOLT® Lock as the recipient of the 2018 NEMPA Yankee Supplier Award. This specific award is given to automotive suppliers who have made
body_text: MILWAUKEE – The New England Motor Press Association (NEMPA) selected BOLT® Lock as the recipient of the 2018 NEMPA Yankee Supplier Award. This specific award is given to automotive suppliers who have made significant contributions to the industry, whether by making driving safer, more cost-efficient or more enjoyable. NEMPA hosts the awards annually in an effort to recognize manufacturers, suppliers and industry professionals who have brought excellence to the automotive industry. Members of NEMPA selected the winner of the supplier award. The awards are tailored to the automotive needs and tastes of New England drivers. The Yankee Supplier Award was presented at NEMPA’s Annual Awards dinner held at the MIT Media Lab in Cambridge, Massachusetts on May 30, 2018. BOLT Lock’s “Breakthrough One-Key Lock Technology” is a unique technological advancement which allows every lock in the product line to be specifically coded to a vehicle’s ignition key. Key-ring clutter is greatly reduced as every cable, coupler, receiver, padlock and more can be locked and unlocked using only the vehicle’s key. “All of us at BOLT Lock are thrilled to receive this award. The technology is a great advancement that makes securing a driver’s valuables simple without any of the headache of searching through to find the right key,” said Steve Gilles, Director of New Business Development for BOLT Lock. BOLT Locks has experienced tremendous growth in the six years since the brand came to market so much so it has earned several prestigious industry awards. To date, BOLT has earned the following awards: Associated Locksmiths of America New Product Showcase – 2009 SEMA Global Media Awards – 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2015 BizTimes I.Q. (Innovation Quotient Awards) 2010 Popular Mechanic’s Editor’s Choice Award - BOLT Coupler Lock - 2013 Best New Product Award in van/pickup/SUV category - SEMA - BOLT J-Mount Jeep High Lift Jack Bracket Mounting System – 2015 About BOLT (Breakthrough One-Key Lock Technology) BOLT locks come with a limited lifetime warranty. Find a BOLT retailer by using the zip code finder at www.boltlock.com/stores . BOLT locks are also available at 4-Wheel Parts stores, AdvanceAutoParts.com , Cabela's, Pep Boys, and SummitRacing.com . For more information, visit www.boltlock.com or call 844.972.7547 . Follow BOLT: Facebook.com/BOLTLock , Instagram: @BOLTLock or Twitter: @BOLTLock.

title: BANCFIRST CORPORATION REPORTS SECOND QUARTER EARNINGS
summary: /PRNewswire/ -- BancFirst Corporation (NASDAQ GS: BANF) reported net income of $66.7 million, or $1.96 per diluted share, for the second quarter of 2026...
body_text: OKLAHOMA CITY , July 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BancFirst Corporation (NASDAQ GS: BANF) reported net income of $66.7 million, or $1.96 per diluted share, for the second quarter of 2026 compared to net income of $62.3 million, or $1.85 per diluted share, for the second quarter of 2025. The Company's net interest income for the three-months ending June 30, 2026 increased to $133.5 million from $121.3 million for the same period in 2025. Higher loan volume and general growth in earning assets were the primary drivers of the change in net interest income. Net interest margin was 3.84% for the second quarter of 2026 compared to 3.75% for the second quarter of 2025. The Company recorded a provision for credit losses of $4.9 million and $1.4 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. Noninterest income for the quarter totaled $53.9 million compared to $48.0 million in the same quarter last year. Trust revenue, service charges on deposits, securities transactions, and treasury income each increased when compared to second quarter of 2025. The Company also recorded gains of $2.9 million related to bank owned life insurance claims during the quarter. The increase in noninterest income was partially offset by a decrease in insurance commissions. Noninterest expense grew to $97.5 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 compared to $88.2 million in the same quarter in 2025. The increase in noninterest expense was primarily attributable to the growth in salaries and employee benefits of $5.2 million. The total salaries and employee benefits expenses recorded of $60.3 million is after a favorable adjustment to the funded employee benefit trust of $800,000. Also driving the increase in noninterest expense was net expense from other real estate owned, which increased $1.6 million period to period. At June 30, 2026, the Company's total assets were $15.1 billion, an increase of $243.4 million from December 31, 2025. Loans grew $110.6 million from December 31, 2025, totaling $8.7 billion at June 30, 2026. Deposits totaled $12.8 billion, an increase of $155.9 million from year-end 2025. Sweep accounts totaled $5.0 billion at June 30, 2026, up $100.8 million from December 31, 2025. The Company's stockholders' equity stood at $2.0 billion, an increase of $103.0 million from the end of 2025. Nonaccrual loans represented 0.94% of total loans at June 30, 2026, up from 0.72% at year-end 2025. Nonaccrual loans totaled $81.4 million at the end of the second quarter 2026. The allowance for credit losses to total loans was 1.25% at June 30, 2026 and 1.22% at December 31, 2025. Net charge-offs totaled $2.4 million for the quarter compared to $4.7 million for the second quarter last year. BancFirst Corporation CEO David Harlow commented, "The Company enjoyed a record quarter fueled by an expanding margin and earning asset growth. Noninterest income growth was solid across most major categories and expenses were managed in line with plan. We announced the acquisition of SpiritBank during the quarter, adding the Tulsa MSA communities of Bristow and Sapulpa while expanding our presence in the Tulsa market. Pending regulatory approval, a fourth quarter close and conversion is anticipated. Our economic outlook continues to be guarded, although charge-offs remain at historically low levels. With a $4.9 million provision during the quarter, our allowance for credit losses remains at a healthy level." BancFirst Corporation (the Company) is an Oklahoma based financial services holding company. The Company operates three subsidiary banks, BancFirst, an Oklahoma state-chartered bank with 109 banking locations serving 62 communities across Oklahoma, Pegasus Bank, a Texas state-chartered bank with three banking locations in the Dallas Metroplex area, and Worthington Bank, a Texas state-chartered bank with three locations in the Fort Worth Metroplex area, one location in Arlington Texas and one location in Denton Texas. More information can be found at www.bancfirst.bank .
